prompt:
Research the following and cite real, verifiable sources:

Research whether there is real published data on the historical resolution accuracy of Polymarket's short-duration crypto up/down markets compared to actual price outcomes. Cite specific sources.
response:
Yes, there is real published data on this, including a 2026 Hugging Face dataset with oracle-settled resolutions and a GitHub research repo that explicitly measures how well the short-duration BTC up/down book matched realized outcomes.

## Best source: oracle-settled historical dataset

The strongest direct source is the Hugging Face dataset **“Polymarket crypto up/down microstructure (5m/15m)”** by `kinzikdza`. It covers **six weeks** of live data from **May 27 to Jun 24, 2026**, for **BTC/ETH/SOL/XRP** 5-minute and 15-minute up/down markets, and crucially says the outcome labels come **only from Polymarket’s gamma `outcomePrices`**, which it calls the authoritative settlement oracle, rather than inferring outcomes from spot. That makes it one of the cleanest public sources for comparing market-implied probabilities to actual resolutions. [huggingface.co](https://huggingface.co/datasets/kinzikdza/polymarket-updown-microstructure)

That dataset also documents exactly why this comparison is nontrivial: the displayed book is often **crossed or phantom**, so the authors warn that the “inside market” should be anchored to **real trades**, not naively to displayed quotes. In other words, there is real resolution data, but measuring accuracy requires care. [huggingface.co](https://huggingface.co/datasets/kinzikdza/polymarket-updown-microstructure)

## Direct accuracy evidence: book vs actual outcome

The most direct published accuracy comparison I found is the GitHub project **Fierdimo/polymarket-analysis**, which studies Polymarket’s **5-minute “Bitcoin Up or Down”** markets and compares predictors against realized outcomes. It reports that, out of sample, the **order-book mid** predicted the actual outcome with **AUC 0.837** and **log-loss 0.491**. That is a concrete historical accuracy result for short-duration crypto up/down markets. [github.com](https://github.com/Fierdimo/polymarket-analysis/blob/main/README.md)

The same repo also says the book mid was **well calibrated to realized `P(Up)`** across the range in its recorded windows. So this is not just trade data; it is an explicit comparison of market prices to realized resolutions. [github.com](https://github.com/Fierdimo/polymarket-analysis/blob/main/README.md)

Its broader conclusion matters too: the authors find **no exploitable public-data taker edge**, which is consistent with the idea that these markets were already pricing outcomes fairly efficiently. They estimate an irreducible transaction-cost barrier of about **1.75 probability points at p=0.5** from fees and spread. [github.com](https://github.com/Fierdimo/polymarket-analysis/blob/main/README.md)

## Additional research-grade source, with an important caveat

There is also **juanandub/polymarket-btc-5m-research**, which computes **Brier score, log loss, expected calibration error, probability buckets, spreads, and time-to-expiry summaries** for BTC up/down 5-minute markets. That is directly relevant to “resolution accuracy vs actual outcomes.” [github.com](https://github.com/juanandub/polymarket-btc-5m-research)

However, this source explicitly warns that it is **research-grade only**, because `price_to_beat` and outcomes are derived from **Binance BTCUSDT 5m open as a proxy**, while **Chainlink remains the official Polymarket settlement source**. So it is useful evidence, but not settlement-grade. [github.com](https://github.com/juanandub/polymarket-btc-5m-research)

Its research summary says the market showed **small calibration errors**, but simple directional betting hypotheses did **not** remain robust under forward validation and execution realism. That supports the interpretation that prices were close to outcome probabilities, even if not perfectly tradable. [github.com](https://github.com/juanandub/polymarket-btc-5m-research)

## Broader context and limitations

A 2026 arXiv paper on Polymarket data stresses that short-horizon crypto up/down markets are structurally distinct from standard binary markets and should not be pooled with other categories when assessing quality. It also notes limitations around resolution data and external validity across Polymarket versions. This is useful as a caution when interpreting any historical accuracy claims. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.04217)

Another 2026 arXiv paper uses Polymarket data for a different purpose, but it shows there is now a growing empirical literature built on large historical Polymarket datasets. It does not directly answer your question as cleanly as the two crypto-up/down-specific sources above, though. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.10400)

## Bottom line

Yes. There is **real published data** comparing Polymarket’s short-duration crypto up/down markets to actual outcomes:

- **Settlement-grade resolution data**: the Hugging Face dataset with gamma-oracle outcomes. [huggingface.co](https://huggingface.co/datasets/kinzikdza/polymarket-updown-microstructure)
- **Direct historical accuracy measurement**: `Fierdimo/polymarket-analysis`, reporting **AUC 0.837 / log-loss 0.491** for the order book versus realized outcomes. [github.com](https://github.com/Fierdimo/polymarket-analysis/blob/main/README.md)
- **Calibration metrics with caveats**: `juanandub/polymarket-btc-5m-research`, useful but proxy-based rather than settlement-grade. [github.com](https://github.com/juanandub/polymarket-btc-5m-research)

So the short answer is: **yes, but the best evidence suggests these markets were already fairly accurate and close to efficient, while truly clean settlement-grade measurement is limited to a small number of recent datasets.**
